candidates.title: Quantifying the hosting capacity value of workload flexibility for AI data centers: A two-stage electricity-computation co-optimization framework
candidates.abstract: Grid connection constraints increasingly limit the expansion of AI data centers, yet the additional hosting capacity enabled by computational workload flexibility remains insufficiently quantified. This paper develops a two-stage electricity--computation co-optimization framework to quantify the individual and coordinated hosting capacity values of spatial and temporal workload flexibility. Data center capacities are determined endogenously, with computational task arrivals scaling with admitted capacity. Spatial routing of eligible interactive requests and temporal deferral of batch workloads are linked to server operation and facility power demand, subject to workload completion requirements and transmission constraints. The first stage maximizes aggregate hosting capacity; the second fixes the resulting site capacities and optimizes annual workload scheduling and generation dispatch to minimize generation and carbon costs. An 8760-hour case study with three data centers on a modified IEEE 118-bus system shows that temporal and spatial flexibility individually increase hosting capacity by 21.26\% and 5.37\%, respectively. Their coordinated use raises hosting capacity from 4635.1~MW to 6231.5~MW, a 34.44\% increase without network reinforcement. The coordinated gain exceeds the sum of the individual gains by 361.9~MW, demonstrating complementarity between spatial migration and temporal deferral. By redistributing computational demand across locations and operating hours, these mechanisms enable fuller utilization of existing transmission capacity. The findings establish workload flexibility as a quantifiable planning resource for accommodating additional data center capacity within existing transmission networks.

candidates.title: N-1 Security constrained Hosting Capacity Assessment for Ultra Large-scale Data Center with Workload Flexibility
candidates.abstract: Transmission network security can substantially alter where large-scale data centers can connect and how much workload flexibility can unlock. This paper develops a hosting-capacity framework that couples computing demand, batch workload scheduling, and N-1 security constraints. A modified IEEE 118-bus case study reveals that two data center sites with identical hosting capacities under normal operation differ by 874.5 MW under the contingencies operation when workload flexibility is enabled. Six-hour batch deferral increases N-1 hosting capacity by up to 24.5\% relative to immediate execution. These gains arise from reducing demand at critical hours while accommodating deferred tasks within subsequent transmission limits and deadlines. At bus 92, a four-hour window captures 90.9\% of the six-hour capacity gain. The findings establish workload flexibility as a location-dependent connection resource whose capacity value requires joint assessment of contingency exposure and deadline constrainted workload recovery, beyond the power reduction available at a single critical hour.

candidates.title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
candidates.abstract: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

candidates.title: eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity Commitments
candidates.abstract: Datacenters can procure electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to energy purchases for individual hours. For LLM services operating within these hourly budgets, maximizing aggregate throughput alone may still leave individual requests waiting or receiving much slower service than desired. Fair serving therefore requires improving service for poorly served requests while reserving electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. To compare service across requests, we define normalized throughput as each request's actual output rate divided by the product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, a positive weight representing its desired service level. Using this measure, we formulate fair serving as leximin optimization under an hourly electricity constraint, prioritizing requests with the lowest normalized throughput. To address this problem, we present eFAIR, an online scheduler that coordinates request dispatching, electricity budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection through a common normalized-throughput target. Specifically, request dispatching prioritizes requests by desired service level and progress; electricity budget allocation reserves electricity for current and expected future work; and frequency selection uses electricity savings to raise GPU frequencies for requests with higher desired service levels. Evaluations on H20 and H200 configurations, each with 32 replicas, show that eFAIR improves the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%-31.0% over the best budget-feasible baseline, while keeping absolute deviations from the hourly electricity commitment below 0.26%. eFAIR also improves throughput balance among concurrent requests and aligns electricity allocation more closely with service demand over time. Together, these results demonstrate how eFAIR improves request-level fairness within an hourly commitment.

candidates.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
candidates.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

candidates.title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
candidates.abstract: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

candidates.title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
candidates.abstract: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

candidates.title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

candidates.title: Modeling and Stability of Power Systems With Coupled Data Center and Grid Dynamics
candidates.abstract: The growing deployment of data centers poses challenges for power-system operation. However, data centers possess flexible resources that can be leveraged to mitigate their impact on the grid and provide grid services. This paper develops a linear-affine dynamic model of a transmission network with multiple data centers, explicitly coupling electromechanical grid dynamics with data center power demand and computational backlog. Grid-aware computing policies are incorporated to represent how data centers adjust their computational power in response to grid frequency deviations and workload backlog. The proposed framework provides a tractable means of investigating the interactions between multiple data centers and the transmission grid and assessing the potential of flexible computing to support power-system stability.

candidates.title: Comparison of Open-Source PSCAD EMT Models for Large-Scale AI Data Centers in Smart Grids
candidates.abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) introduces gigawatt-scale, highly nonlinear, and fast-varying electronic loads that challenge grid voltage regulation, frequency stability, and disturbance ride-through. Capturing their transient behavior during grid faults and rapid computational workload swings requires high-fidelity electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations rather than root mean square models. However, limited methodologies exist to audit the component-level adequacy of EMT AIDC models. This paper proposes a software-agnostic, 41-point fidelity framework spanning 11 categories that synthesizes 37 criteria from an existing modeling guideline with four novel requirements: frequency ride-through compliance, disaggregated fan and chiller cooling loads, temperature-dependent thermal response, and DC information technology (IT) load representations. Applying this framework to the four publicly available AIDC models in PSCAD/EMTDC reveals varying degrees of completeness: while the models capture IT load transitions, uninterruptible power supplies, and transfer switches for bulk stability studies, critical gaps remain in electro-thermal cooling coupling, internal protective relaying, and site-level controls. Addressing these gaps will enable comprehensive protection coordination and ride-through compliance studies.

candidates.title: Profile Screening and Frequency-Secure Operating Limit Derivation for Data Center Microgrids
candidates.abstract: Rapid power variations from artificial intelligence (AI) workloads pose frequency-security challenges for islanded data-center microgrids. This paper proposes a generator step- response-based framework to rapidly screen candidate load pro- files and derive frequency-secure operating limits for IT workload scheduling. Identified generator responses are superimposed to assess the cumulative frequency effects of successive load changes without repeated dynamic simulations. The framework identifies potentially unsafe intervals and determines allowable load magni- tudes, ramp rates, and minimum event spacing, while accounting for prediction uncertainty and governor limits. Validation on a 2.5 MVA islanded microgrid with eight generator configurations and 14 synthetic AI workload profiles shows that 94.75% of 40,208 assessment windows receive decisive screening labels, with no frequency-violating windows classified as secure.
